span.label: whether a penetrating electrode array in the inferior colliculus can restore useful hearing, and what stimulating different midbrain regions reveals about how the human auditory system is organised
span.quote: The goal of this study has been (1) to demonstrate the safety and evaluate the efficacy of the AMI for hearing restoration and (2) to better understand the functional organization of the human central auditory system, which will help us improve future AMI designs and stimulation strategies. We will discuss findings associated with level coding, tonotopy, temporal coding, and sound localization pathways within the human midbrain.

span.label: whether stimulating along the tonotopic gradient of the human central nucleus produces ordered pitch percepts, as it does along the cochlea
span.quote: One motivation for selecting the IC as a target site for an auditory prosthesis is the well defined tonotopic organization of its central nucleus. This has been shown extensively in animal models ( Schreiner and Langner, 1997 ; Oliver, 2005 ), and, because of the similarities in the anatomical structure of the IC across mammalian species ( Geniec and Morest, 1971 ), it was inferred that such a functional organization exists within the human ICC. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated previously in a guinea pig model that more localized frequency-specific activation is achievable for ICC stimulation than cochlear stimulation ( Lenarz et al., 2006a ; Lim and Anderson, 2006 ). Based on these findings, it was hypothesized that stimulation along the tonotopic gradient of the human ICC would elicit ordered pitch percepts similar to what has been observed for stimulation along the tonotopically organized cochlea. However, this has not yet been the case.

span.label: the implant is safe and gives loudness, temporal and directional percepts and speech benefit comparable with the brainstem implant, but the ordered pitch the whole rationale predicted did not appear
span.quote: We recently implanted three patients with the auditory midbrain implant (AMI), and it has proven to be safe with minimal movement over time. The AMI provides loudness, pitch, temporal, and directional cues, features that have shown to be important for speech perception and more complex sound processing. Thus far, all three patients obtain enhancements in lip reading capabilities and environmental awareness and some improvements in speech perception comparable with that of NF2 ABI patients.

span.label: method
span.quote: These limitations have motivated us to develop a new hearing prosthesis that stimulates the midbrain with a penetrating electrode array.

span.label: auditory midbrain implant for hearing restoration
span.quote: We recently implanted three patients with the auditory midbrain implant (AMI), and it has proven to be safe with minimal movement over time.

span.label: system-or-tool-building
span.quote: We have begun clinical trials in which three NF2 patients have been implanted with the AMI.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Sustained stimulation rates and patterns overdrive adaptation-prone neurons in the dorsal IC, raising the current needed over time
span.quote: One hypothesis is that the stimulation rates and patterns are overdriving the neurons located within the dorsal IC region

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Neurons higher in the auditory pathway lose the ability to phase-lock, and that loss of temporal synchronization is traded for a spatial, spike-rate-based code of temporal features, which is why the midbrain follows lower rates than the fibre pathway below it
span.quote: This degradation in temporal synchronization is hypothesized to be compensated for by spatial coding (based on spike rate) of temporal features

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Ipsilaterally and contralaterally driven brainstem projections stay segregated as they ascend into the IC, so which region the array sits in determines the perceived direction of the sound
span.quote: AMI-2 and AMI-3 obtained all ipsilateral and contralateral percepts, respectively, suggesting some segregation of ipsilateral and contralateral pathways ascending into and within the IC.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The ipsilaterally excited fibre population is dominated by low-frequency-tuned neurons, so stimulating it yields low-pitch percepts
span.quote: Most of the ipsilaterally excited pathways consist of neurons sensitive to low-frequency sounds, which would explain the dominance of low pitches perceived by AMI-2.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: An array lying outside the IC acts as a surface electrode, so current must travel further to reach neurons and activation levels rise
span.quote: The array in AMI-2 is placed outside of the IC (ventral to the dorsal nucleus of the lateral lemniscus) similar to a surface array and likely requires higher current levels to activate neurons farther away.

span.label: the central nucleus is chosen because it receives almost all ascending brainstem pathways, so it should give access to a more complete set of inputs than the cochlea or cochlear nucleus
span.quote: Our animal studies ( Lim and Anderson, 2003 , 2006 ; Lenarz et al., 2006a ) have shown that the inferior colliculus (IC), particularly its central nucleus (ICC), has potential as a new site for an auditory prosthesis. In particular, ICC stimulation achieves lower thresholds, greater dynamic ranges, and more localized, frequency-specific cortical activation than CI stimulation. The IC also receives inputs from almost all brainstem pathways projecting to higher perceptual centers ( Casseday et al., 2002 ). Thus, it should provide direct access to a more complete set of pathways necessary for complex processing and binaural percepts than occurs in the cochlear nucleus or cochlea for the ABI or CI, respectively.

span.label: the limited performance of tumour patients with the brainstem implant is attributed to tumour damage in the cochlear nucleus, which is the argument for moving upstream
span.quote: Recently, the ABI has been implanted in nontumor patients who would not benefit from CIs (e.g., such as those with nerve avulsion/aplasia and cochlear ossification). Surprisingly, some of these patients achieve performance levels comparable with CI patients, suggesting that the limited performance of NF2 ABI patients may be attributed to some tumor-related damage within the cochlear nucleus ( Colletti and Shannon, 2005 ). Thus, a site proximal to this damaged region may be better for an auditory prosthesis.

span.label: segregated monaural and binaural pathways ascending into the midbrain are proposed to explain why each patient perceived only one direction
span.quote: In other words, it is more likely to find neurons excited solely by contralateral sounds in the dorsomedial region of the ICC. This could explain why we observed only contralateral percepts for AMI-3. The findings for AMI-2 further suggest that a segregated group (or at least a predominance) of ipsilaterally excited projections to the IC exist within the ventral portion of the lateral lemniscus in humans. Considering that the medial olivary nucleus is enlarged whereas the lateral olivary nucleus is reduced in humans compared with animals ( Moore, 1987 ) and only a small proportion of ipsilaterally excited pathways to the IC appear to originate from the cochlear nucleus and periolivary region, this segregated region may correspond predominantly to fibers from the medial superior olive

span.label: ipsilaterally driven pathways carry mostly low frequencies, which is offered as the reason one patient heard only low pitches
span.quote: Most of the ipsilaterally excited pathways consist of neurons sensitive to low-frequency sounds, which would explain the dominance of low pitches perceived by AMI-2.

span.label: temporal synchrony degrades at successive stages of the pathway, so a site below the colliculus should follow faster rates - which is what happened
span.quote: Animal studies have shown that auditory nerve fibers can synchronize to high-rate (exceeding 1 kHz) acoustic ( Johnson, 1980 ; Joris and Yin, 1992 ) and cochlear ( Hartmann and Klinke, 1989 ; Shepherd and Javel, 1997 ) stimulation, whereas neurons higher along the auditory pathway are less able to follow high-rate stimulation ( Phillips et al., 1989 ; Lu and Wang, 2000 ; Snyder et al., 2000 ). This degradation in temporal synchronization is hypothesized to be compensated for by spatial coding (based on spike rate) of temporal features ( Schreiner and Langner, 1988 ; Lu et al., 2001 ). The fact that AMI-2, who was implanted at the level of the lateral lemniscus, was able to detect a buzzing percept beyond 200 pps that was almost three times greater than the rates of the other patients implanted into the IC is consistent with this hypothesis. However, it is also possible that the sites for AMI-1 and AMI-3 are just located in regions of low temporal resolution. In guinea pigs, stimulation of more caudal and dorsal regions along an ICC lamina, in which AMI-3 is implanted, elicits auditory cortical activity with longer latencies and greater spiking jitter ( Lim and Anderson, 2007 ). Both explanations emphasize the need for appropriate placement and/or more complex spatial stimuli within the ICC to achieve enhanced coding of temporal features.

span.label: long shallow loudness tails are read as a non-homogeneous mix of excitatory and inhibitory neurons along the isofrequency dimension
span.quote: It is also interesting that loudness growth functions for AMI-3 ( Fig. 6 C ) exhibited long shallow tails in which a very soft sound was heard over a wide range of stimulus levels relative to the dynamic range that then rapidly elevated in loudness. These findings suggest a nonhomogenous organization of excitatory and inhibitory neurons along the isofrequency dimension of the ICC.

span.label: rising activation levels in one patient are hypothesised to be neurons in the dorsal region being overdriven by the stimulation pattern
span.quote: The activation levels for AMI-1 ( Fig. 2 A ) were initially some of the lowest from the three patients. Note that the T and C levels presented in Figure 1 A for +4 d (from when implant was first turned on) are approximate values. The actual measured values were unavailable, and the modified values used for daily stimulation are shown. Over time, the T and C levels for AMI-1 continued to rise, reaching the compliance voltage of our stimulator (at +125 d). Because of this rise in levels, we turned off the processor for 48 d to assess whether levels would return to usable levels. The activation levels decreased dramatically but not completely to the initial values. It is not clear as to what may be causing these adaptive effects.

span.quote: Although the common tests for temporal resolution are amplitude modulation detection and gap detection, we could not perform these tests with our software.

span.label: loudness balancing across the different sites and pulse rates was difficult because of limitations in the testing software, and performance on this test was argued to depend on whether the patient could clearly hear the sound rather than on slight variations in loudness

During psychophysical tests, we instructed the patients to ignore the tinnitus and focus on the test stimulus.

The alignment of the array with respect to the ICC layers were determined by comparing the fused images and fixed slices with stained midbrain sections presented by Geniec and Morest (1971) .

span.quote: Are there particular stimuli, both temporally and spatially, required to elicit higher pitch percepts than a simple pulse train at one ICC location (we used pulse rates up to 2400 pps without any obvious increase in pitch from that of 250 pps)?

span.label: the paper then lists four rival explanations as open questions - the stimulus form, plastic loss of high frequency representation after six years of deafness, position along the isofrequency dimension or passing fibres, and species differences - and chooses none

Five ABI patients performed worse than AMI-1 and AMI-2 (less than two to three words per minute). All had zero speech tracking scores with the ABI alone.

Similarly, site 1 always had a lower pitch percept than site 5 in AMI-3. However, the variability across days (even different times on the same day) demonstrates the difficulty for these patients in consistently differentiating the pitch between sites. For example, in AMI-3 (Rank +2 d), stimulation of sites 3 and 11 elicited much higher pitch percepts in the morning than in the afternoon. This variability is much greater than what we typically observe for our CI patients.

span.label: pitch —operationalised-as→ environmental sounds
span.note: with no reference tone available the scale is built from familiar environmental sounds, and most sites came out below a man's voice
span.quote: Interestingly, all three patients stated that stimulation of their sites generally elicited low pitch sounds. To confirm this, we performed a pitch test with an absolute scale in which different numbers (0–5) corresponded to familiar environmental sounds having different pitches. Data from AMI-2 and AMI-3 are presented in Figure 5 in which stimulation of most of their sites elicited a pitch percept lower than a man's voice, with only a few sites approaching that of a woman's voice. At least in AMI-3, it was expected that some of the deeper sites would elicit higher pitch percepts. AMI-1 had difficulties in scaling the sounds, yet we were able to compare pitch percepts from AMI stimulation to those produced by pure tone stimulation in her right ear (residual hearing up to 1 kHz with thresholds between 30 and 50 dB HL). We found that stimulation of all her sites elicited pitch percepts that were lower than 1 kHz. The narrow range of pitches, thus the small differences in pitch between sites, partly explains why the patients had difficulty in consistently ordering the pitch percepts across sites. However, this raises another question as to why stimulation of all their sites elicited predominantly low pitches.

span.label: pitch —distinct-from→ ICC
span.note: and for the one correctly aligned array the deviation from the predicted low-to-high order is left unexplained
span.quote: For AMI-2, a lack of a clear systematic spatial pitch organization is not surprising because the array is not aligned along any obvious tonotopic gradient. span.label: deaf —causes→ plastic

span.quote: Considering that AMI-3 was deaf for 6 years before implantation, could plastic reorganization of the auditory system result in a loss of high-frequency representation, and, if so, what does this mean for implementing different stimulation strategies across patients with varying deafness conditions? span.label: array placement —causes→ percept
span.note: THE ACCIDENT IS THE INDEPENDENT VARIABLE: three arrays in three different places, and that unintended variation is what turns a safety trial into a map
span.quote: One fortunate outcome of our different array placements across patients is that we could assess the effects of various stimuli in specific midbrain regions on perceptual effects, which provide some insight into how the human central auditory system is functionally organized and how we may need to implement an AMI.

span.label: sites —operationalised-as→ ICC
span.note: the plan was 45 degrees off the sagittal plane so that sites would fall in different anatomical layers, which supposedly correspond to frequency laminas
span.quote: Our intention was to insert the array 45° off the sagittal plane perpendicular to the IC surface and into the ICC to position the sites within different anatomical layers ( Geniec and Morest, 1971 ), which supposedly correspond to different frequency laminas based on animal studies

span.label: electrode array —part-of→ sites
span.note: 20 ring electrodes at 200 micrometre spacing over 6.2 mm, numbered from the base to the tip
span.quote: The array is 6.2 mm long with a diameter of 0.4 mm. It consists of 20 platinum ring electrodes linearly spaced at an interval of 200 μm. Each site has a thickness of 100 μm (surface area of ∼126,000 μm 2 ). A stainless steel stylet is positioned through the axial center of the silicone carrier to enable insertion of the array into the brain and is removed after placement. Additional details on the AMI electrode array have been provided previously ( Lenarz et al., 2006b ). For our analyses and plots, we ordered the array sites from 1 to 20, with 20 being the tip site.

span.label: sites —causes→ paresthesia

span.quote: The array in AMI-3 was inserted ∼45° from the sagittal plane with a slight caudal-to-rostral orientation relative to the surface of the right IC. The array was inserted into the caudal and dorsomedial portion of the ICC based on anatomical results presented by Geniec and Morest (1971) . Sites 12–20 were positioned into deeper nonauditory regions and elicited paresthesia in the contralateral thigh, leg, and foot.

span.quote: In AMI-2, the array was inserted ∼90° from the sagittal plane below the right IC at the level of the dorsal nucleus of the lateral lemniscus in which fibers ascending into the IC are located. Based on human anatomical data ( Geniec and Morest, 1971 ; Moore, 1987 ), the sites were positioned near the ventral edge of the lateral lemniscus (and close to nonauditory structures) acting more as surface electrodes. As a result, stimulation of all sites elicited a mixture of auditory and nonauditory sensations, of which the latter consisted of paresthesia and cold sensations in the contralateral face and upper body.

span.quote: In brief, no patients experienced any pain or adverse functional effects attributable to AMI implantation or stimulation. They experienced some uncomfortable side effects to AMI stimulation ( Table 1 ) that could be avoided by inactivating certain sites.

span.quote: One fortunate outcome of our different array placements across patients is that we could assess the effects of various stimuli in specific midbrain regions on perceptual effects, which provide some insight into how the human central auditory system is functionally organized and how we may need to implement an AMI.

span.quote: AMI-1, who was implanted in the dorsal IC region, perceived binaural sounds for stimulation of all active sites ( Fig. 3 ). AMI-1 expressed that the loudness percept sometimes varied between sides but not in any obvious manner with stimulation site or level. AMI-2, who was implanted more on the ventral surface of the lateral lemniscus, perceived ipsilateral sounds for all active sites. Usually for the inactive sites but sometimes for the active sites at suprathreshold levels, AMI-2 perceived low vibrations in the contralateral ear that did not appear to be sound sensations. AMI-3, who appears to be implanted within a more caudal and dorsomedial region of the ICC, perceived only contralateral sounds.

span.note: and the percept does not vary across the 1.7 to 1.9 mm the active sites span, which is the argument for segregated ascending pathways
span.quote: Stimulation of all active sites (spanning 1.7–1.9 mm) elicited the same directional percept in each patient. AMI-1 obtained all bilateral percepts, which could be caused by activation of monaural and binaural neurons throughout the dorsal and commissure of the IC ( Malmierca et al., 2005 ; Saldana and Merchan, 2005 ). AMI-2 and AMI-3 obtained all ipsilateral and contralateral percepts, respectively, suggesting some segregation of ipsilateral and contralateral pathways ascending into and within the IC.

span.quote: The IC receives both monaural and binaural projections from different brainstem nuclei, and it is thought that these projections maintain some segregation up to and within the IC ( Cant, 2005 ; Schofield, 2005 ). Thus, it is expected that stimulation of different midbrain regions should elicit varying directional percepts.

span.note: the inference runs from a human anatomical asymmetry - enlarged medial and reduced lateral olive - to which fibres one array must have been sitting among
span.quote: In other words, it is more likely to find neurons excited solely by contralateral sounds in the dorsomedial region of the ICC. The findings for AMI-2 further suggest that a segregated group (or at least a predominance) of ipsilaterally excited projections to the IC exist within the ventral portion of the lateral lemniscus in humans. Considering that the medial olivary nucleus is enlarged whereas the lateral olivary nucleus is reduced in humans compared with animals ( Moore, 1987 ) and only a small proportion of ipsilaterally excited pathways to the IC appear to originate from the cochlear nucleus and periolivary region, this segregated region may correspond predominantly to fibers from the medial superior olive

span.note: and the same anatomy is then used to explain that patient's low pitches, so one placement accounts for two separate anomalies
span.quote: Most of the ipsilaterally excited pathways consist of neurons sensitive to low-frequency sounds, which would explain the dominance of low pitches perceived by AMI-2.

span.label: temporal resolution —operationalised-as→ pulse rate
span.note: THE MEASURE IS A SUBSTITUTE: modulation and gap detection could not be run because the software would not do them, so the rate at which pulses fuse into a continuous sound is used instead
span.quote: Although the common tests for temporal resolution are amplitude modulation detection and gap detection, we could not perform these tests with our software. Instead, we stimulated a given site with continuous pulse trains that varied in pulse rate and determined the highest rate at which the individual pulses, perceived as buzzing, began to sound continuous

span.quote: Animal studies have shown that auditory nerve fibers can synchronize to high-rate (exceeding 1 kHz) acoustic ( Johnson, 1980 ; Joris and Yin, 1992 ) and cochlear ( Hartmann and Klinke, 1989 ; Shepherd and Javel, 1997 ) stimulation, whereas neurons higher along the auditory pathway are less able to follow high-rate stimulation ( Phillips et al., 1989 ; Lu and Wang, 2000 ; Snyder et al., 2000 ). This degradation in temporal synchronization is hypothesized to be compensated for by spatial coding (based on spike rate) of temporal features ( Schreiner and Langner, 1988 ; Lu et al., 2001 ). The fact that AMI-2, who was implanted at the level of the lateral lemniscus, was able to detect a buzzing percept beyond 200 pps that was almost three times greater than the rates of the other patients implanted into the IC is consistent with this hypothesis. However, it is also possible that the sites for AMI-1 and AMI-3 are just located in regions of low temporal resolution. In guinea pigs, stimulation of more caudal and dorsal regions along an ICC lamina, in which AMI-3 is implanted, elicits auditory cortical activity with longer latencies and greater spiking jitter ( Lim and Anderson, 2007 ). Both explanations emphasize the need for appropriate placement and/or more complex spatial stimuli within the ICC to achieve enhanced coding of temporal features.

The actual measured values were unavailable, and the modified values used for daily stimulation are shown. Because of this rise in levels, we turned off the processor for 48 d to assess whether levels would return to usable levels. span.quote: In brief, no patients experienced any pain or adverse functional effects attributable to AMI implantation or stimulation. They experienced some uncomfortable side effects to AMI stimulation ( Table 1 ) that could be avoided by inactivating certain sites.

span.label: inferior colliculus —contrasted-with→ cochlear nucleus
span.note: the target is chosen because nearly all ascending pathways converge there, so it should give access to a more complete set of inputs
span.quote: Our animal studies ( Lim and Anderson, 2003 , 2006 ; Lenarz et al., 2006a ) have shown that the inferior colliculus (IC), particularly its central nucleus (ICC), has potential as a new site for an auditory prosthesis. In particular, ICC stimulation achieves lower thresholds, greater dynamic ranges, and more localized, frequency-specific cortical activation than CI stimulation. The IC also receives inputs from almost all brainstem pathways projecting to higher perceptual centers ( Casseday et al., 2002 ). Thus, it should provide direct access to a more complete set of pathways necessary for complex processing and binaural percepts than occurs in the cochlear nucleus or cochlea for the ABI or CI, respectively.

span.label: auditory brainstem implant —operationalised-as→ cochlear nucleus
span.quote: These patients can be implanted with the auditory brainstem implant (ABI), which stimulates the surface of the cochlear nucleus. Unfortunately, the ABI has achieved limited success in its main patient group [i.e., those with neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)] and requires a difficult surgical procedure. These limitations have motivated us to develop a new hearing prosthesis that stimulates the midbrain with a penetrating electrode array.

span.label: cochlear nucleus —causes→ NF2
span.note: THE CLUE THAT MOVED THE TARGET: non-tumour patients do as well as cochlear implant users on the same device, which puts the blame on tumour damage rather than on the site
span.quote: Recently, the ABI has been implanted in nontumor patients who would not benefit from CIs (e.g., such as those with nerve avulsion/aplasia and cochlear ossification). Surprisingly, some of these patients achieve performance levels comparable with CI patients, suggesting that the limited performance of NF2 ABI patients may be attributed to some tumor-related damage within the cochlear nucleus ( Colletti and Shannon, 2005 ). Thus, a site proximal to this damaged region may be better for an auditory prosthesis.

span.label: cochlear implant —operationalised-as→ auditory nerve
span.quote: More than 100,000 patients worldwide suffering from severe to profound hearing loss have been implanted with a cochlear implant (CI). The CI converts acoustic sound into electrical stimulation patterns that are transmitted to the cochlea to excite the remaining auditory nerve fibers. Many CI patients routinely converse over the telephone ( Adams et al., 2004 ). Thus, they achieve intelligible speech perception without lip-reading cues.

span.label: midbrain —contrasted-with→ cochlear nucleus
span.note: the new target against the existing one - the whole clinical claim is a comparison with the alternative these patients would otherwise receive
span.quote: These patients can be implanted with the auditory brainstem implant (ABI), which stimulates the surface of the cochlear nucleus. Unfortunately, the ABI has achieved limited success in its main patient group [i.e., those with neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)] and requires a difficult surgical procedure. These limitations have motivated us to develop a new hearing prosthesis that stimulates the midbrain with a penetrating electrode array.

span.note: the clinical endpoint is an ENHANCEMENT of lip reading rather than hearing on its own
span.quote: We recently implanted three patients with the auditory midbrain implant (AMI), and it has proven to be safe with minimal movement over time. The AMI provides loudness, pitch, temporal, and directional cues, features that have shown to be important for speech perception and more complex sound processing. Thus far, all three patients obtain enhancements in lip reading capabilities and environmental awareness and some improvements in speech perception comparable with that of NF2 ABI patients.

span.label: Patients detected every test instrument but could only identify the low-frequency ones, mirroring the absence of high-pitch percepts.
span.quote: Both were able to detect all instruments. However, they could only identify the low-frequency instruments.

span.label: THE FOUNDING PREDICTION FAILED: ordered pitch along the tonotopic gradient was hypothesised from animal work, and did not appear
span.quote: One motivation for selecting the IC as a target site for an auditory prosthesis is the well defined tonotopic organization of its central nucleus. This has been shown extensively in animal models ( Schreiner and Langner, 1997 ; Oliver, 2005 ), and, because of the similarities in the anatomical structure of the IC across mammalian species ( Geniec and Morest, 1971 ), it was inferred that such a functional organization exists within the human ICC. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated previously in a guinea pig model that more localized frequency-specific activation is achievable for ICC stimulation than cochlear stimulation ( Lenarz et al., 2006a ; Lim and Anderson, 2006 ). Based on these findings, it was hypothesized that stimulation along the tonotopic gradient of the human ICC would elicit ordered pitch percepts similar to what has been observed for stimulation along the tonotopically organized cochlea. However, this has not yet been the case.

span.label: stimulation of nearly all sites in all three patients gave low pitch percepts, below a man's voice
span.quote: Interestingly, all three patients stated that stimulation of their sites generally elicited low pitch sounds. To confirm this, we performed a pitch test with an absolute scale in which different numbers (0–5) corresponded to familiar environmental sounds having different pitches. Data from AMI-2 and AMI-3 are presented in Figure 5 in which stimulation of most of their sites elicited a pitch percept lower than a man's voice, with only a few sites approaching that of a woman's voice. At least in AMI-3, it was expected that some of the deeper sites would elicit higher pitch percepts. AMI-1 had difficulties in scaling the sounds, yet we were able to compare pitch percepts from AMI stimulation to those produced by pure tone stimulation in her right ear (residual hearing up to 1 kHz with thresholds between 30 and 50 dB HL). We found that stimulation of all her sites elicited pitch percepts that were lower than 1 kHz. The narrow range of pitches, thus the small differences in pitch between sites, partly explains why the patients had difficulty in consistently ordering the pitch percepts across sites. However, this raises another question as to why stimulation of all their sites elicited predominantly low pitches.

span.label: and pulse rates up to 2400 per second produced no obvious rise in pitch over 250
span.quote: Are there particular stimuli, both temporally and spatially, required to elicit higher pitch percepts than a simple pulse train at one ICC location (we used pulse rates up to 2400 pps without any obvious increase in pitch from that of 250 pps)?

span.label: pitch scores varied across days and even across different times on the same day, variability much greater than what is typically observed for CI patients
span.quote: As is evident from both plots, there is some general shift in pitch scores with the sites reordered. For example, site 16 always had a lower pitch percept than site 17 in AMI-2. Similarly, site 1 always had a lower pitch percept than site 5 in AMI-3. However, the variability across days (even different times on the same day) demonstrates the difficulty for these patients in consistently differentiating the pitch between sites. For example, in AMI-3 (Rank +2 d), stimulation of sites 3 and 11 elicited much higher pitch percepts in the morning than in the afternoon. This variability is much greater than what we typically observe for our CI patients.

span.label: for the one correctly aligned array the deviation from the predicted order is left unexplained
span.quote: For AMI-2, a lack of a clear systematic spatial pitch organization is not surprising because the array is not aligned along any obvious tonotopic gradient. However, it is still not clear for AMI-3 as to what may be causing the variability in pitch ordering across sessions and the deviation from the low-to-high pitch ordering expected for stimulation of more superficial sites (excluding the most superficial sites, which could be in the external nucleus) to deeper sites within the ICC as predicted from animal models.

span.label: FOUR RIVAL EXPLANATIONS ARE LISTED AS OPEN QUESTIONS and none is chosen: stimulus form, plastic loss of high frequency representation after six years of deafness, position along the isofrequency dimension or passing fibres, and species differences
span.quote: Considering that AMI-3 was deaf for 6 years before implantation, could plastic reorganization of the auditory system result in a loss of high-frequency representation, and, if so, what does this mean for implementing different stimulation strategies across patients with varying deafness conditions? Are high pitch percepts even necessary for speech perception or is it only important to achieve a consistent pitch order? Is the lack of a clear pitch order attributable to location of stimulation along the isofrequency dimension of the ICC, caused by activation of passing fibers with mixed tonotopy, or even associated with differences in auditory midbrain organization in behaving primates?

span.label: AND NO DEFINITIVE CLAIM IS MADE about human midbrain tonotopy, because only one patient's array was aligned along the gradient
span.quote: Because we only have pitch data for one patient whose array is supposedly aligned along the tonotopic gradient of the ICC, we cannot make any definitive claims as to the tonotopy within the human midbrain until more patients are implanted.

span.label: AMI thresholds and dynamic ranges are similar to those of the CI, though the sites are in direct contact with surrounding neurons and thresholds should be lower
span.quote: AMI sites are in direct contact with surrounding neurons, unlike CI sites; thus, thresholds should be lower as shown in animal studies ( Lim and Anderson, 2003 , 2006 ; Lenarz et al., 2006a ). However, AMI thresholds (only for AMI-3 whose sites are in the ICC) are 6–12 nC (5–10 μC/cm 2 ), and dynamic ranges are 7–9 dB, which are similar to those of the CI

span.label: and the animal explanation offered for that is questioned in the same paragraph
span.quote: It is possible, as shown in guinea pigs ( Lim and Anderson, 2007 ), that stimulation of more caudal and dorsal regions along the ICC laminas, in which the array is located in AMI-3, requires higher current levels for auditory cortical activation than stimulation of more rostral and ventral regions (>17 dB at the extreme edges). However, this then raises the question as to why stimulation of a caudodorsal ICC region would require higher current levels when sites are in close contact to neurons.

span.label: all patients gave monotonically increasing loudness with current, so level cues are transmissible
span.quote: All patients exhibited monotonically increasing loudness curves with increasing current levels.

span.label: one patient showed long shallow loudness tails, read as a non-homogeneous mix of excitatory and inhibitory neurons along the lamina
span.quote: It is also interesting that loudness growth functions for AMI-3 ( Fig. 6 C ) exhibited long shallow tails in which a very soft sound was heard over a wide range of stimulus levels relative to the dynamic range that then rapidly elevated in loudness. These findings suggest a nonhomogenous organization of excitatory and inhibitory neurons along the isofrequency dimension of the ICC.

span.label: ONE DIRECTION PER PATIENT: binaural throughout for the dorsal placement, ipsilateral throughout for the lemniscal one, contralateral throughout for the central nucleus one
span.quote: AMI-1, who was implanted in the dorsal IC region, perceived binaural sounds for stimulation of all active sites ( Fig. 3 ). AMI-1 expressed that the loudness percept sometimes varied between sides but not in any obvious manner with stimulation site or level. AMI-2, who was implanted more on the ventral surface of the lateral lemniscus, perceived ipsilateral sounds for all active sites. Usually for the inactive sites but sometimes for the active sites at suprathreshold levels, AMI-2 perceived low vibrations in the contralateral ear that did not appear to be sound sensations. AMI-3, who appears to be implanted within a more caudal and dorsomedial region of the ICC, perceived only contralateral sounds.

span.label: and the direction did not change across the 1.7 to 1.9 mm the active sites span
span.quote: Stimulation of all active sites (spanning 1.7–1.9 mm) elicited the same directional percept in each patient. AMI-1 obtained all bilateral percepts, which could be caused by activation of monaural and binaural neurons throughout the dorsal and commissure of the IC ( Malmierca et al., 2005 ; Saldana and Merchan, 2005 ). AMI-2 and AMI-3 obtained all ipsilateral and contralateral percepts, respectively, suggesting some segregation of ipsilateral and contralateral pathways ascending into and within the IC.

span.label: which is taken as human support for segregated monaural and binaural pathways derived from animal work
span.quote: Overall, our results support the animal-derived hypothesis of segregated monaural/binaural pathways within the central auditory system and demonstrate the importance of stimulation location within the midbrain for achieving different sound localization percepts.

span.label: the ipsilateral percepts are attributed to medial superior olive fibres, using the enlarged medial and reduced lateral olive of humans
span.quote: In other words, it is more likely to find neurons excited solely by contralateral sounds in the dorsomedial region of the ICC. This could explain why we observed only contralateral percepts for AMI-3. The findings for AMI-2 further suggest that a segregated group (or at least a predominance) of ipsilaterally excited projections to the IC exist within the ventral portion of the lateral lemniscus in humans. Considering that the medial olivary nucleus is enlarged whereas the lateral olivary nucleus is reduced in humans compared with animals ( Moore, 1987 ) and only a small proportion of ipsilaterally excited pathways to the IC appear to originate from the cochlear nucleus and periolivary region, this segregated region may correspond predominantly to fibers from the medial superior olive

span.label: and the same placement is used to explain that patient's low pitches, since ipsilaterally driven pathways carry mostly low frequencies
span.quote: Most of the ipsilaterally excited pathways consist of neurons sensitive to low-frequency sounds, which would explain the dominance of low pitches perceived by AMI-2.

span.label: pulses fused into a continuous sound above 80 per second and usually near 50, a resolution of about 20 ms, against 250 to 300 for cochlear stimulation
span.quote: Normal hearing subjects can hear individual noise bursts for repetition rates up to 40 Hz that then fuse into a continuous percept above ∼250 Hz ( Miller and Taylor, 1948 ). For cochlear and auditory nerve stimulation, patients can hear the pulses of a pulse train perceived as a buzzing for rates up to 250–300 pps ( Simmons et al., 1964 , 1965 ; Shannon, 1985 ). Thus, the brain is wired to allow detection of temporal features of sound with a resolution down to a few milliseconds (<4 ms) for both normal hearing ( Plomp, 1964 ) and CI ( Shannon, 1989 ) subjects. However, when stimulating within the IC, our patients perceived a continuous stimuli for pulse rates above 80 pps, with most cases at ∼50 pps, which corresponds to a resolution of ∼20 ms.

span.label: the patient implanted below the colliculus followed about three times the rate of the other two
span.quote: For AMI-1 and AMI-3, who were both implanted in the IC, a buzzing percept continued up to ∼35–80 pps, with a mean ± SD of 42 ± 7 and 65 ± 8 pps, respectively. Interestingly, AMI-2 was able to detect a buzzing percept up to 220 pps (mean ± SD, 180 ± 17), which was about three times the rate of the other patients.

span.label: TWO INCOMPATIBLE READINGS OF THAT ARE BOTH KEPT: synchrony degrading up the pathway, or the other two arrays simply sitting in regions of poor temporal resolution
span.quote: Animal studies have shown that auditory nerve fibers can synchronize to high-rate (exceeding 1 kHz) acoustic ( Johnson, 1980 ; Joris and Yin, 1992 ) and cochlear ( Hartmann and Klinke, 1989 ; Shepherd and Javel, 1997 ) stimulation, whereas neurons higher along the auditory pathway are less able to follow high-rate stimulation ( Phillips et al., 1989 ; Lu and Wang, 2000 ; Snyder et al., 2000 ). This degradation in temporal synchronization is hypothesized to be compensated for by spatial coding (based on spike rate) of temporal features ( Schreiner and Langner, 1988 ; Lu et al., 2001 ). The fact that AMI-2, who was implanted at the level of the lateral lemniscus, was able to detect a buzzing percept beyond 200 pps that was almost three times greater than the rates of the other patients implanted into the IC is consistent with this hypothesis. However, it is also possible that the sites for AMI-1 and AMI-3 are just located in regions of low temporal resolution. In guinea pigs, stimulation of more caudal and dorsal regions along an ICC lamina, in which AMI-3 is implanted, elicits auditory cortical activity with longer latencies and greater spiking jitter ( Lim and Anderson, 2007 ). Both explanations emphasize the need for appropriate placement and/or more complex spatial stimuli within the ICC to achieve enhanced coding of temporal features.

span.label: THE ACCIDENT IS THE INDEPENDENT VARIABLE: three arrays landed in three different places, and that variation is what makes the trial a map of the auditory midbrain
span.quote: One fortunate outcome of our different array placements across patients is that we could assess the effects of various stimuli in specific midbrain regions on perceptual effects, which provide some insight into how the human central auditory system is functionally organized and how we may need to implement an AMI.

span.label: the intention was to insert the array 45 degrees off the sagittal plane and into the ICC to position the sites within different anatomical layers, which supposedly correspond to different frequency laminas
span.quote: Our intention was to insert the array 45° off the sagittal plane perpendicular to the IC surface and into the ICC to position the sites within different anatomical layers ( Geniec and Morest, 1971 ), which supposedly correspond to different frequency laminas based on animal studies

span.label: deep sites in the first patient caused dizziness and chest and facial sensations and were switched off
span.quote: The parasagittal section (top) of Figure 1 B shows that the array was inserted in the rostral portion of the IC with a caudal-to-rostral rather than a perpendicular orientation relative to the IC surface. The axial section (bottom) shows that the array was inserted through the dorsal cortex of the IC with an ∼45° angle. The end of the array extends into nonauditory regions. As a result, stimulation of deeper sites (sites 12–20) elicited dizziness and sensations in the chest and contralateral face and were not used for daily stimulation.

span.label: the second array sat below the colliculus near the lateral lemniscus and every site mixed auditory with cold and paresthetic sensations
span.quote: In AMI-2, the array was inserted ∼90° from the sagittal plane below the right IC at the level of the dorsal nucleus of the lateral lemniscus in which fibers ascending into the IC are located. Based on human anatomical data ( Geniec and Morest, 1971 ; Moore, 1987 ), the sites were positioned near the ventral edge of the lateral lemniscus (and close to nonauditory structures) acting more as surface electrodes. As a result, stimulation of all sites elicited a mixture of auditory and nonauditory sensations, of which the latter consisted of paresthesia and cold sensations in the contralateral face and upper body.

span.label: the third array reached the intended central nucleus, with deep sites producing paresthesia in the contralateral thigh, leg and foot
span.quote: The array in AMI-3 was inserted ∼45° from the sagittal plane with a slight caudal-to-rostral orientation relative to the surface of the right IC. The array was inserted into the caudal and dorsomedial portion of the ICC based on anatomical results presented by Geniec and Morest (1971) . Sites 12–20 were positioned into deeper nonauditory regions and elicited paresthesia in the contralateral thigh, leg, and foot.

span.label: no pain or adverse functional effect resulted, and uncomfortable percepts were removed by switching sites off
span.quote: In brief, no patients experienced any pain or adverse functional effects attributable to AMI implantation or stimulation. They experienced some uncomfortable side effects to AMI stimulation ( Table 1 ) that could be avoided by inactivating certain sites.

span.label: the auditory sensations and side effects associated with each site have generally remained stable, indicating minimal movement of the implant over time
span.quote: The other two patients exhibited stable activation levels over time ( Fig. 2 B , C ), suggesting that location of stimulation, thus the type of neurons activated, is important for AMI implementation. The auditory sensations and/or side effects associated with each site have generally remained stable, indicating minimal movement of the implant over time.

span.label: but the levels for AMI-1 continued to rise, reaching the compliance voltage of the stimulator, so the processor was turned off for 48 d, after which the activation levels decreased dramatically but not completely to the initial values
span.quote: The activation levels for AMI-1 ( Fig. 2 A ) were initially some of the lowest from the three patients. Note that the T and C levels presented in Figure 1 A for +4 d (from when implant was first turned on) are approximate values. The actual measured values were unavailable, and the modified values used for daily stimulation are shown. Over time, the T and C levels for AMI-1 continued to rise, reaching the compliance voltage of our stimulator (at +125 d). Because of this rise in levels, we turned off the processor for 48 d to assess whether levels would return to usable levels. The activation levels decreased dramatically but not completely to the initial values. It is not clear as to what may be causing these adaptive effects.

span.label: speech benefit at six months was comparable with eleven brainstem implant patients tested in the same clinic by the same speech therapist
span.quote: Speech results in the AMI patients, particularly for AMI-3 who is implanted in the intended target (ICC), are comparable with what are observed in ABI NF2 patients at 6 months. Of 11 ABI NF2 patients tested in our clinic using the same protocols (the same speech therapist tested all the ABI and AMI patients) ( Lenarz et al., 2001 ), only four exceeded the 11 words per minute enhancement achieved by AMI-3. Five ABI patients performed worse than AMI-1 and AMI-2 (less than two to three words per minute). All had zero speech tracking scores with the ABI alone.

span.label: and the brainstem group's own scores span a wide range, with six of eleven getting no consonant benefit at all
span.quote: Vowel and consonant scores were also comparable between AMI and ABI patients, although the latter exhibited a greater range of scores across more patients. Lip-reading enhancement in ABI patients ranged between −4 and 40%, with more than half being below 15%. In ABI alone mode, vowel scores were ∼45% on average, whereas consonant scores were ∼10%, which is consistent with what was observed for AMI-3. Six of the 11 ABI patients did not receive any benefit for ABI alone in the consonant test.

span.label: two patients scored above chance on vowels with the implant alone
span.quote: For the vowel test ( Fig. 8 A ), all three patients achieved high scores for lip reading alone, making it difficult to detect significant lip-reading enhancement with the AMI. However, AMI-2 and AMI-3 obtained 23 and 40% correct (10% chance level), respectively, with the AMI alone, indicating that they are obtaining some speech information with their implants.

span.label: both tested patients detected every instrument but could identify only the low frequency ones
span.quote: In addition to speech tests, we also assessed the ability of AMI-2 and AMI-3 to detect and discriminate different instrumental sounds (low frequency: drum, melodica, xylophone, and wooden sticks; high frequency: triangle, ringing bell, jingling bell, and shaker). We randomly played different instruments and asked whether they could detect and identify each one. Both were able to detect all instruments. However, they could only identify the low-frequency instruments. Occasionally, they identified the triangle but generally could not discriminate among the high-frequency instruments.

span.label: and the reported gains are in everyday awareness - traffic, birds, doors, the telephone - and in one patient's control of her own voice
span.quote: More importantly, they have all expressed improvements in their awareness of environmental sounds, such as cars driving by, birds chirping, doors shutting, and the telephone ringing. We have observed the most rapid improvements in AMI-3. The other two patients are improving more slowly because of their dependence on residual hearing and the location of their implants. Before implantation, AMI-3 had difficulties in controlling the volume of her voice. She is now able to speak at a consistent loudness level, has improved the articulation of words, and no longer depends on written conversations.

span.label: the stimulus parameters were chosen at the point where more charge stopped lowering thresholds and less charge raised them sharply
span.quote: Briefly, 250 pps was high enough to avoid noticeable rate pitch effects (i.e., increasing rates up to 2400 pps did not noticeably increase the pitch from that at 250 pps) and the lowest rate available for daily stimulation to minimize adaptive effects. These parameters also achieved the largest drop in thresholds in which using longer pulse widths and higher pulse rates (thus greater total charge) did not decrease thresholds by much more, whereas using shorter pulse widths and slower pulse rates substantially increased threshold levels.

span.label: and those slices are read against fixed and stained human midbrain sections from an anatomical collection

span.label: 220 pps (mean ± SD, 180 ± 17) — temporal fusion rate for the patient implanted at the lateral lemniscus
span.quote: Interestingly, AMI-2 was able to detect a buzzing percept up to 220 pps (mean ± SD, 180 ± 17), which was about three times the rate of the other patients.

span.label: 23 and 40% correct (10% chance level) — vowel identification with AMI stimulation alone for AMI-2 and AMI-3 at 6 months
span.quote: However, AMI-2 and AMI-3 obtained 23 and 40% correct (10% chance level), respectively, with the AMI alone, indicating that they are obtaining some speech information with their implants.

span.label: 12.5 and 10% — consonant and number test scores achieved above chance by AMI-3 with the implant alone
span.quote: only AMI-3 performed above chance with the AMI alone (12.5 and 10%, respectively)

span.label: ∼2–11 words per minute — lip-reading enhancement in speech tracking obtained by adding the AMI to lip reading
span.quote: For both AMI and lip reading, they obtained a lip-reading enhancement of ∼2–11 words per minute (chance level of 0).

span.label: ∼85–100 words per minute — speech tracking rate of normal-hearing subjects in the same clinic, as a reference
span.quote: Normal hearing subjects tested in our clinic achieve ∼85–100 words per minute

span.label: only four — number out of 11 ABI NF2 patients who beat AMI-3's 11 words-per-minute lip-reading enhancement
span.quote: only four exceeded the 11 words per minute enhancement achieved by AMI-3

span.label: 2400 pps — pulse rates swept this high without any obvious increase in pitch over 250, which closes the most obvious escape from the failed prediction
span.quote: Are there particular stimuli, both temporally and spatially, required to elicit higher pitch percepts than a simple pulse train at one ICC location (we used pulse rates up to 2400 pps without any obvious increase in pitch from that of 250 pps)?

span.label: 7–9 dB — dynamic range in the correctly placed patient, similar to the cochlear implant rather than better as animal work predicted
span.quote: AMI sites are in direct contact with surrounding neurons, unlike CI sites; thus, thresholds should be lower as shown in animal studies ( Lim and Anderson, 2003 , 2006 ; Lenarz et al., 2006a ). However, AMI thresholds (only for AMI-3 whose sites are in the ICC) are 6–12 nC (5–10 μC/cm 2 ), and dynamic ranges are 7–9 dB, which are similar to those of the CI

span.label: ∼20 ms — the temporal resolution implied by fusion near 50 pulses per second, against a few milliseconds for cochlear stimulation
span.quote: Normal hearing subjects can hear individual noise bursts for repetition rates up to 40 Hz that then fuse into a continuous percept above ∼250 Hz ( Miller and Taylor, 1948 ). For cochlear and auditory nerve stimulation, patients can hear the pulses of a pulse train perceived as a buzzing for rates up to 250–300 pps ( Simmons et al., 1964 , 1965 ; Shannon, 1985 ). Thus, the brain is wired to allow detection of temporal features of sound with a resolution down to a few milliseconds (<4 ms) for both normal hearing ( Plomp, 1964 ) and CI ( Shannon, 1989 ) subjects. However, when stimulating within the IC, our patients perceived a continuous stimuli for pulse rates above 80 pps, with most cases at ∼50 pps, which corresponds to a resolution of ∼20 ms.

span.label: 1.7–1.9 mm — the span of active sites across which the perceived direction never changed
span.quote: Stimulation of all active sites (spanning 1.7–1.9 mm) elicited the same directional percept in each patient. AMI-1 obtained all bilateral percepts, which could be caused by activation of monaural and binaural neurons throughout the dorsal and commissure of the IC ( Malmierca et al., 2005 ; Saldana and Merchan, 2005 ). AMI-2 and AMI-3 obtained all ipsilateral and contralateral percepts, respectively, suggesting some segregation of ipsilateral and contralateral pathways ascending into and within the IC.

span.label: 48 d — how long the device was switched off after one patient's levels reached the stimulator's compliance voltage
span.quote: The activation levels for AMI-1 ( Fig. 2 A ) were initially some of the lowest from the three patients. Note that the T and C levels presented in Figure 1 A for +4 d (from when implant was first turned on) are approximate values. The actual measured values were unavailable, and the modified values used for daily stimulation are shown. Over time, the T and C levels for AMI-1 continued to rise, reaching the compliance voltage of our stimulator (at +125 d). Because of this rise in levels, we turned off the processor for 48 d to assess whether levels would return to usable levels. The activation levels decreased dramatically but not completely to the initial values. It is not clear as to what may be causing these adaptive effects.

span.label: 6.2 mm — array length, carrying 20 sites at 200 micrometre spacing
span.quote: The array is 6.2 mm long with a diameter of 0.4 mm. It consists of 20 platinum ring electrodes linearly spaced at an interval of 200 μm. Each site has a thickness of 100 μm (surface area of ∼126,000 μm 2 ). A stainless steel stylet is positioned through the axial center of the silicone carrier to enable insertion of the array into the brain and is removed after placement. Additional details on the AMI electrode array have been provided previously ( Lenarz et al., 2006b ). For our analyses and plots, we ordered the array sites from 1 to 20, with 20 being the tip site.

span.label: 11 ABI NF2 patients — the comparison group, tested in the same clinic under the same protocols by the same speech therapist
span.quote: Speech results in the AMI patients, particularly for AMI-3 who is implanted in the intended target (ICC), are comparable with what are observed in ABI NF2 patients at 6 months. Of 11 ABI NF2 patients tested in our clinic using the same protocols (the same speech therapist tested all the ABI and AMI patients) ( Lenarz et al., 2001 ), only four exceeded the 11 words per minute enhancement achieved by AMI-3. Five ABI patients performed worse than AMI-1 and AMI-2 (less than two to three words per minute). All had zero speech tracking scores with the ABI alone.
